o99: 'Algo' means something: a thing, not a person (Quiero comer algo). A person is 'alguien' (someone). 'Algún' / 'alguno' means some and goes with a noun (algún día).
o100: Use 'este' before a noun: este café (this coffee). It is the masculine form; the feminine is 'esta' (esta casa). 'Esto' is a different word: it stands alone for something you do not name, and never goes before a noun.
o156: Use 'ese' before a noun: ese hombre (that man). It is the masculine form; the feminine is 'esa' (esa casa). 'Eso' is a different word: it stands alone for something you do not name, and never goes before a noun.
o157: Use 'esto' on its own, for a thing or a situation you do not name: Esto es muy bueno (This is very good). It never goes before a noun. Before a noun use 'este' or 'esta': este café, esta casa.
o158: Use 'eso' on its own, for a thing or a situation you do not name: Eso no es un problema (That is not a problem). It never goes before a noun. Before a noun use 'ese' or 'esa': ese hombre, esa casa.
o163: 'Alguien' means someone: a person (Alguien está en la puerta). A thing is 'algo' (something). 'Algún' / 'alguno' means some and goes with a noun (algún día). 'Alguien' never changes.
o261: Same meal, two English words. 'Dinner' is the usual word today; 'supper' is an older or more regional word for the evening meal (in some places a lighter, later one). Spanish needs only one: la cena.
o603: 'Camisa' is a shirt: it has buttons down the front and a collar (Mi padre tiene una camisa nueva). A jacket you put on over your clothes when it is cold is 'la chamarra'. English 'shirt' = camisa; 'jacket' = chamarra. A T-shirt is 'la playera'.
o701: 'Algún' / 'alguno' means some and goes with a noun: algún día (some day). 'Algún' stands before a masculine singular noun; 'alguna' is the feminine (alguna vez). A thing alone is 'algo' (something), a person is 'alguien' (someone).
o770: 'Estómago' is the organ inside the body, the stomach (it digests food). The belly you see from outside, the everyday 'tummy', is 'la barriga'. English 'stomach' = estómago; 'belly' or 'tummy' = barriga.
o969: 'Chamarra' is a jacket: you put it on over your clothes when it is cold (Hace frío y necesito una chamarra). A shirt with buttons and a collar is 'la camisa'. English 'jacket' = chamarra; 'shirt' = camisa.
o1026: 'Reír' is to laugh, with sound (Mi hermano y yo siempre reímos). 'Sonreír' is to smile, with no sound, only the mouth. English 'laugh' = reír; 'smile' = sonreír.
o1054: 'Sonreír' is to smile, with no sound, only the mouth (Mi madre sonríe cuando me ve). 'Reír' is to laugh, out loud. English 'smile' = sonreír; 'laugh' = reír.
o1492: 'Barriga' is the belly seen from outside, the everyday word (belly, tummy). 'Estómago' is the organ inside the body, the stomach. English 'belly' or 'tummy' = barriga; English 'stomach' = estómago.
o1610: In the example sentence, 'al' is just 'a' + 'el' written as one word (Spanish never writes 'a el'). The 'a' is there because gustar works as 'is pleasing to': 'a el mono le gusta...' = 'to the monkey it is pleasing'. The word itself is el mono.
o2771: A Mexican dish: a corn tortilla dipped in chili sauce, rolled around a filling (often chicken or cheese) and covered with red or green sauce, cheese and cream. You usually see it in the plural: las enchiladas.
